prime.problem: A GPU has tens to hundreds of SMs and needs hundreds of thousands of threads to stay busy, but you can't write a separate program for each. Without a model of how one kernel is cut into blocks and warps, you can't tell which threads may share data, which can sync, or why some branches cost double.
prime.fits: First card after the overview. perf-1's GPU-as-a-machine card showed the hardware (SMs, registers, HBM); this card is the programming model that maps your code onto it. Every later card, from coalescing to Triton, is about what 32 lanes of a warp do together.
prime.goal: Compute any thread's global index, warp and lane; say how many blocks fit per SM and how many waves a launch takes; and explain why blocks can't wait for each other inside a kernel.

attend: Why must a block live on one SM from start to finish, and what does that buy its threads that different blocks never get?
What goes wrong if one block spins waiting for another block's result, and what does CUDA offer instead of a grid-wide barrier?
Thread 37 of block 3 is warp 1, lane 5: which built-in variables and which rule give you that?
Why does a 50/50 branch on threadIdx.x % 2 cost 16 warp passes per 256-thread block, but a 50/50 branch on (threadIdx.x / 32) % 2 cost only 8?
The same 4,096-block grid takes 26 rounds on a T4 and 4 on an H100. Which two per-SM limits set that, and what would change it?

must: A block runs whole on one SM → its threads share on-chip shared memory and can call __syncthreads() → blocks get no co-scheduling guarantee → no block may wait on another inside a kernel → the kernel boundary is the only grid-wide barrier
Blocks run in any order on any SM → the same grid runs unchanged on 40 or 132 SMs, just in more or fewer waves → scaling to new GPUs is free, but only if blocks are independent

A warp issues one instruction for 32 lanes → lanes that disagree at a branch run each path in turn with the others masked → cost depends on whether both paths occur within a warp, not on how many threads take each path
Resident blocks per SM = min(max threads/SM ÷ block size, max blocks/SM), then registers and shared memory can only lower it → blocks in flight = that × SMs → waves = grid ÷ blocks in flight
elevated: Since Volta, threads have their own program counters (independent thread scheduling) → lanes of a warp are not guaranteed to run in lock-step → old warp-synchronous tricks without __syncwarp are unsafe on both the T4 and the H100
reference: per-CC limits: T4 1,024 threads / 32 warps / 16 blocks per SM; H100 2,048 / 64 / 32
memory-space sizes (64 KB vs 228 KB shared memory, 512 KB local per thread, 64 KB constant)
cluster sizes (8 portable, 16 opt-in on H100) and the GPC

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory, explain what a block is for: what its threads can do together that separate blocks can't, and why CUDA refuses to let blocks wait on each other. Then draw grid → block → warp → thread with one number on each level for the 1,048,576-element vector add.
checklist: a block is a group of threads guaranteed to share one SM, so it can share memory and synchronise
blocks run in any order, so they must be independent; the next kernel launch is the global sync
a warp is 32 consecutive threads issuing one instruction; divergence inside a warp serialises the paths
4,096 blocks × 256 threads = 8 warps each, 32,768 warps, 1,048,576 threads
independence is what lets one grid run in 26 waves on a T4 and 4 on an H100

retrieve.q: Explain why CUDA gives threads in a block a barrier but gives blocks in a grid none, in terms of what the scheduler promises about each.
answer: all threads of a block are resident on one SM at the same time, so a barrier can't deadlock
a grid may have far more blocks than can be resident; a waiting block can block the one it waits for from ever being scheduled
so cross-block dependencies are expressed by ending the kernel and launching another

retrieve.q: Walk through launching add<<<4096, 256>>> on a T4: how many blocks start at once, how many rounds it takes, and how full the last round is.
answer: resident blocks per SM = min(1,024 ÷ 256, 16) = 4; × 40 SMs = 160 in flight
the last round has 96 blocks, 60% full
the idealised picture assumes blocks start in index order; CUDA promises no order

retrieve.q: You must pick a block size for a simple elementwise kernel. Compare 32, 256 and 1,024 threads per block on a T4: what does each cost or risk?
answer: 32: the 16-blocks-per-SM limit caps the SM at 512 threads (50% of its slots)
256: 4 blocks fill all 1,024 thread slots; the guide's usual starting point
1,024: one block per SM fills it too, but any register or shared-memory growth drops you to zero or one block, and a block can't exceed 1,024
non-multiples of 32 waste lanes in the last warp (100 threads → 4 warps, 28 idle lanes)

compare.q: CUDA's SIMT model vs Triton's blocked programs: what is the unit you write code for in each, which design choice moves coalescing and shared memory from you to the compiler, and when does each model fail you?
answer: CUDA: code for one thread, launched as blocks of threads; Triton: code for one block of data, the compiler picks threads
seeing the whole block's data flow lets Triton's compiler choose the thread layout, vector width and shared-memory staging
CUDA fails you in effort and bookkeeping; Triton fails you when you need per-thread control or the newest hardware features first

compare.q: perf-1 described the SM as hardware; this card describes the block as software. Which hardware limits turn into the software rules here, and what breaks if you ignore each?
answer: threads/SM and blocks/SM limits → resident blocks and waves
register file size → registers per thread × threads per block must fit, or the launch fails
shared memory per SM → how many blocks can share an SM
ignoring them: failed launches, or fewer blocks in flight than you expected

predict.q: Same 1,048,576-element launch, but with 32-thread blocks. Commit before revealing: how many waves on a T4 and on an H100, and why is it worse than 64-thread blocks even though both are whole warps?
predict.answer: T4: min(1,024 ÷ 32, 16) = 16 resident blocks per SM (the 16-block limit bites), so only 512 threads per SM, 640 blocks in flight, and 32,768 ÷ 640 = 51.2 waves instead of 25.6. H100: min(64, 32) = 32 blocks, 1,024 threads per SM (50%), 4,224 in flight, 7.76 waves instead of 3.88. With 64-thread blocks the thread limit and block limit meet exactly, so both GPUs fill every thread slot.

apply.task: Run labs/execution-model.py (or do it by hand) for N = 1,048,576 with block sizes 32, 64, 128, 256 and 1,024 on the T4 (40 SMs, 1,024 threads, 16 blocks per SM) and the H100 (132 SMs, 2,048 threads, 32 blocks per SM). Tabulate resident blocks per SM, threads per SM and waves. Then write two versions of a 256-thread kernel with a 25/75 branch, one on threadIdx.x % 4 == 0 and one on (threadIdx.x / 32) % 4 == 0, and count warp passes per block in each.
apply.done: Your table shows every block size from 64 up gives 25.6 waves on the T4 and 3.88 on the H100, while 32 gives 51.2 and 7.76; and your branch count is 16 passes for the lane-wise split vs 8 for the warp-wise split.
apply.hint: Only the lane-wise split puts both paths inside every warp. The warp-wise one sends whole warps down one path: 2 warps take the if and 6 the else, one pass each.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 32-thread waves, or the divergence count?

Which relationship is still fuzzy: per-SM limits → resident blocks, or resident blocks → waves?
Where in the later cards do you expect "what 32 lanes do together" to matter most: memory or branches?
